winner.title: Shorpo (Soup)

evidence.authenticity: Published by a Kyrgyz-focused organization in a Kyrgyz recipe collection. Fries the meat in oil or mutton fat, then simmers with radish, tomato and dill, which fits the regional versions. No background text and no named author.
evidence.precision: 2 lb meat cut into 2-inch chunks, 8 cups water, 1/2 cup dill, 1/2 tsp red pepper. Doneness cues are 'meat is soft' and 'potatoes soft' (2 cues). Produce is counted, not sized or weighed. No pot size and no meat browning time.
evidence.testing: No test notes and no reasoning given.
evidence.photos: One 150x150 thumbnail of the finished dish. No process photos.
evidence.efficiency: Seven short steps with sensible staging: potatoes go in late, and the 1.5 to 2 hour simmer is stated realistically.
evidence.access: All ingredients are available at a US grocery. Substitutions given for meat, fat and tomato (paste or fresh).

winner.why: It is the most traditional-looking method (brown the meat, then simmer, with dill and radish) from a Kyrgyz source, but it is thin on precision, testing and photos.

runnerUp.title: Shorpo

evidence.authenticity: Generic Central Asian shorpo with bone-in lamb, potato, carrot and dill. Gives a short roots blurb but is not Kyrgyz-specific.
evidence.precision: 2 lb / 900 g lamb, 2.4 L water, produce sized (4 medium potatoes, 3 large carrots). Sensory cues in 2 steps (skim impurities, vegetables tender). No pot size and no weights for the produce.
evidence.photos: No step images in the schema. 3 images on the page.
evidence.efficiency: Simple 8 steps. The 1.5 hour simmer is realistic.

runnerUp.why: Better sizing and a metric conversion, but it is less region-specific and does not brown the meat.

searches: Kyrgyz shorpo recipe lamb broth potatoes dill cilantro blog
notes: Nothing from the test-kitchen sites; both sites searches found no matches. Every English recipe is a short, untested blog or community-page recipe, and none gives weights for the produce, pot sizes, or process photos. Best next step if one is needed: a Russian-language source with grams and photos (for example a Kyrgyz food site), or use the Kyrgyz Children's Future method and add the doneness cues by hand. Some pages found in search were skipped as unreliable (hellskitchen sslip.io mirror, food.com/geniuskitchen copies, Wikipedia). The Taste of Asia page's claim of being served at every Kyrgyz family lunch is unsourced.
